utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness B, I just want to quickly follow up two matters that we spoke about yesterday. Firstly in connection with your military service, when you served in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what type of military unit did you serve in; in other words, infantry, artillery, signals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you achieve any rank of any kind above that of private soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The second matter I just want to ask you about is the Serb prisoners who were detained at Keraterm whom you were eventually able to recall for us. It's right, isn't it, that at least one, if not more, were detained at Keraterm because they had mistreated detainees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now, please, to the interrogation which was conducted of you in Keraterm. How soon after your arrest was the interrogation carried out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been some 8 days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you know the persons who were interrogating you? Did you know their names? Were you told their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct that the -- was it a single individual interrogating you or more than one person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was interrogated by one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And did you learn from him or learn from some other source that he was a policeman, an inspector in the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The questions which you were asked, did they fall into these categories: First of all, questions about your politics and whether you had been involved in politics in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They asked me what was I doing during those days, what did I know about people who had weapons or did this or that, that is, they were mostly interested in developments before Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct in relation to interrogations as a whole, that if a detainee was suspected of having taken part, for example, in military activity or some activity considered dangerous to the Serb authorities, they were subsequently taken to Omarska; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It could be.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [redacted], there were two occasions when you were beaten, and the reasons why you were beaten was firstly because you were -- would not find and would not name two extremists for the policeman who showed you his ID card; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And on the second occasion because a fellow prisoner could not physically get out to be beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness B. I want now to just turn to other beatings and the motives for those. The beating of the man Car, the focus of the animosity towards him was the allegation that he had been arrested in possession of a machine-gun; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I heard. I don't know if that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, I understand that you obviously weren't there. That was what you heard was the cause of the beating. The next one is Fajzo. I'm not sure if that's the correct pronunciation, witness B. Did you know of the reason for his beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't beat Faca. Faca beat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I'm talking about the man who was cut with a knife across his neck.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fajzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My fault for not being a very good pronouncer of your language, and I apologise, Witness B. You'll have to forgive me. Did you hear what the reasons for the assault on him was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear something, that Knezevic's brother had been killed, and that it had to do with that. Who had killed him, I don't know. I heard that it was a Serb who had killed him and that Knezevic also killed him afterwards and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Emsud Bahonjic, who was beaten by Zigic and Duca, did you hear what the reason for that beating was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came from the area of Kozarac and he was told that he had had a sniper, but on his death bed he swore to me by everything dear to him that he never had a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Then the beating of an Albanian person called Jasmin, is this correct, that the reason why he was ill-treated was there was some jealousy or dispute about the bakery which he ran near the railway station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the reason. All I know is that he was called out and beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would this be correct, Witness B, that many beatings were carried out by people who wanted to extort money from detainees or who wanted to settle old scores or repay old debts from before the conflict? Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And for example, Zigic, who was I think a guard for a very short period of time, he lost his job because of his behaviour towards detainees, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And he in particular used to pick on detainees whom he had known before the war, former colleagues and so on, with whom he wanted to settle old accounts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mostly pounced upon detainees from the area of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is it right that he would come to the camp and ask a detainee, for example, to provide within a defined time limit money or gold or watches, and that if he didn't get anything, he would then beat detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And after his dismissal from the camp, he would return usually at night to commit further beatings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was detained but he left the -- his place of detention whenever he liked. Allegedly he fired shots and wounded a man. I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you know who it was who procured his removal from the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but as likely as not the major part was played by Kajin because he was the one who helped most at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct, that there were frequently occasions when either guards or shift commanders would intervene to stop or prevent beatings from taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't intervene frequently but he is not quite normal person.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now, please, to the incident involving Room 3 which you have described to Their Honours. Before the shooting started that night, is it right that you heard singing and shouting from Room 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That was after 9.00 at night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You told Their Honours yesterday that you had been locked up and that nobody was looking outside at all and that you could only hear what was going on. At what time had you been locked up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that day, I think we were locked up a little bit earlier because obviously something was afoot, and everybody knew that something was going to happen. But I wouldn't know the time, because the time had stopped for all of us at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. What time were you normally locked up at night?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And you think that on this occasion you had been locked up earlier than 9.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I think it -- yes, that it was before 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And is it your position that after being locked up, you saw nothing else of what happened outside the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. No, I didn't see anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why, then, did you tell the Office of the Prosecutor in January 1995 that after 9.00 p.m., you describe in your statement what happened after 9.00 p.m., "They started -- prisoners in Room 3 started singing and were yelling. They broke the windows in their room. After the prisoners broke the windows, they started throwing prisoners out of the window. I do not know if the prisoners were alive or dead. Around this time, I saw a bus with some soldiers on it arrive at the camp."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Do you remember telling the Office of the Prosecutor that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have. But at that time there is a small portion which we could see the entrance into the camp which we could see from Room 4, and that is because the door to our room did not close completely so we could see some of this. And we saw some movement there, but we did not see these events. We could hear, however, the door being opened or closed, somebody being put in that room or what is being said because that was quite near.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So when you say you didn't see anything else, that's not entirely true, is it? You did see other things. Why didn't you tell us that in the first place, Witness B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what the statement says should be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: After the incident had taken place the following day, did you come to know anything of the role in the incident of Zivko Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that. All I do know is that I heard that he had come, and that after that, Kole threw his rifle away. But that is what I heard. I don't know if that really happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Briefly just one thing about the beatings which took place on the 26th of July, Witness B, that was carried out by the Banovic brothers and somebody whose name you didn't know; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes. I know that they had a hand in that, but I do not know exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: About a week or so before the closure of the camp at Keraterm, a new warden, upravnik, was appointed to be in charge; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: His name was Marinko Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And so on the date of the closure of the camp, the person in charge of what happened there was that person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as the prisoners, detainees, who were sent to Omarska, how do you personally know that they were sent to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those men were indeed sent to Omarska. And what I said was that those two buses went to Omarska and people saw them. They saw them get off, and those others boarded the buses and came to Trnopolje with them, and they saw that these buses were stained with blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you help me, please, about the lists which you prepared. This is correct, is it not, most of the people on those lists, 90 per cent or more, survived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say so. Yes, you could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you be able, by looking at those lists again, to identify from them those whom you say were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: About some, yes. About others, those who went to Omarska, I wouldn't be able to say anything because I don't know what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like him to do that, if possible. It may be time-consuming to have it done here in court. I wonder whether it would be possible for him to agree to do it after he's completed his evidence and then to hand it through to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We could have it done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I think that would be time saving rather than him sitting there poring through lists and writing out names. I think that would be a sensible way to do it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you continue, I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, please stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are not attired for the purpose of discharging your functions in this courtroom. You are excused so as to get yourself properly attired.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And please don't let it happen again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness B. I'd like you to do that after you've completed your evidence, if you would be so kind, and if you would be so kind to hand that, I think, to Mr. Mundis who is in charge of you and he will then hand it through to us. Finally, witness B, I want to ask two questions. The first is this: As far as Dusko Sikirica is concerned would you accept this: That in general, he would be found and keep himself over at the hut which was near to the gate of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, yes. He spent a lot of time in that hut, but he also spent a lot of time outside the hut.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as you being told what his role was when you first got to the camp, again you can't recall who it was who told you that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It could have been Kajin or somebody else. We asked around and we learned what we wanted to know, and of course we wanted to know who was the person in charge there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I suggest to you that the title which was given to you was that he was commander of security; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly. What I know, he was the commander of those three on the shifts. That is the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I suggest to you that you're not right about that, that you're mistaken as to what his role was. In fact, his role was commander of security, meaning commander of the perimeter fence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not for you to ask questions. Answer the questions asked of you by counsel or by the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can I ask him a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just help us with this, Witness B. What did you see Mr. Sikirica doing at the camp, from which you might be able to form a judgement about what his role was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever I needed something -- whenever we needed something, for instance, if we needed a doctor in the camp, I had to go to Sikirica and ask for that doctor, or anything else. Whenever we needed something, for instance, we would tell Kole, Kajin or Fustar, but whenever it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. something of some importance, then it was Sikirica we went to. And I never noticed that he was anything else except a commander of those others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions, thank you very much, subject of course to him providing that list, which I think he should sign. I think that would be helpful, if Your Honour is agreeable to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He could sign it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness B. I am Goran Rodic, attorney from Podgorica and I'm part of the counsel of Mr. -- representing Mr. Damir Dosen, called Kajin. Let me first ask you regarding your yesterday's evidence, when -- during your examination in chief, when answering to the Prosecutor's questions, you said that you moved in the same circle with Kajin, and I would like to ask you where it was that you went out together and where you saw each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I could express myself better. We were not part of the same circle but we moved -- we would meet in the same coffee bars, same places.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In this socialising or in seeing each other in these various coffee bars, was there any difference between the two of you on any basis?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: These groups in coffee bars where you would see Kajin and other people, were these groups composed of people from various ethnic backgrounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you also gave evidence about cooperation and friendship between Cirkin Polje and Donja Puharska.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Given that the accused Kajin is also from Cirkin Polje, can you tell me whether he too was part of this socialising, and how was that expressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was from the youth gatherings, sports, working together, young people from these communities gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did Mr. Kajin participate in that? Did you see him there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions regarding Keraterm now. What I'm interested in is when was Kajin at Keraterm and when he was there, did he try to alleviate your conditions? In other words, did he allow you to stay outside of the room? Did he allow you access to water and things like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He even drove us to see a physician if anybody needed it. He would -- made a van available for that. He always did that. Fortunately for us, things were good when Kajin was around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is not in the record. Did I understand you well to have said that a van was made available that would take them -- that would take the prisoners to visit a physician?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there was a van around there which, as needed, was used to drive prisoners. I don't know whether it was always there, whether they called in for this van, but there was a van there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Kajin was the one who organised this, who --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to know him and he talked nicely to us so we were not afraid of him. So we went to him when we needed something. He always did whatever we -- he could for us, as much as he could, provide water, help us get medical treatment, whatever we needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During his shift were you able to be outside of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: During his shift, yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me during your stay at Keraterm, did you see Kajin beating anyone or mistreat anyone while he was at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard from one person, but I don't know whether that was true or not. He should say. I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in his presence, were any of the prisoners beaten or mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, did you see or hear whether he ever issued an order for someone to be mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, during your examination-in-chief, you also said that after a period of time, you transferred from Room 1 to Room 4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And in that connection, you mentioned Kajin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My question to you is whether Kajin's suggestion to move from one room to another, you understood as his attempt to improve the conditions under which you were housed in Room 1, given the overcrowdedness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we were better off there. We also felt safer and we felt that we were under his protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether it ever happened that Kajin, as your superior leader, in a way, did he ever ask you to collect any money for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you know Kajin's brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drazan, I met him in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was Kajin's brother also known by the same nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people did, and some people called him by his first name. He was a very fine fellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But if I understand you correctly, you also heard some people address him as Kajin too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was Kajin's brother, and you said that his name was Drazan, working in the same shift with Damir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this throughout your stay in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He worked in the same shift with him before these 12-hour shifts were created. I think that at first there were 24-hour shifts in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was Kajin's brother's behaviour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: He behaved well. I had asked him to bring some styrofoam, and he allowed me, and we went there to get it together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you needed this styrofoam?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: We placed the styrofoam on the concrete and so we could use it for sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I am going to ask you a question now, and please remember not to mention any names. Was your brother also imprisoned in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And again, without mentioning any names, could you tell me what period of time this covered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 31st to the 5th of August, the same period of time when I was detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me in which room he was housed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was housed in the same room where I was, in Room 4, and we went through the same procedure. We were interrogated and after the interrogation, we were moved and we ended up in Room 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, first it was -- he was in Room 2, then Room 1 and, in the end, Room 4; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether your brother was beaten or mistreated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was both beaten and mistreated. This was done by Keli and a relative of Zoran Karlica and some other man who he did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you say how many times this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was taken out once.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person who was part of the guards' security detail who went by the nickname of Crni, and if I can also maybe add that he was driving a motorcycle before the war. He was -- the height was about 170 and he had a nickel-plated pistol.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to remember some things but some things escape me so let me not say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you at least tell us what sounds familiar regarding this Crni?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Regarding the accused Dosen, I would like to ask you something about his character, from your acquaintance with him, both from before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything bad about him. While we were young, we were all a little bit wild. I guess people sort of become mature with age and -- but my experiences of him are -- were most relevant relating to the camp, and I can say what I heard from his neighbour, and it was a fine family. His character was on the level.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The record is not reflecting all -- what did you hear from the neighbour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard very nice things about the whole family. I don't know their parents. Perhaps I know the -- I knew the father slightly but both -- I meet both Damir and Drazen. I got to know them better in the camp and I have no objection or complaint about what they did. Perhaps there were some things that happened in his shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me just take you back a little bit. When you said that your brother was beaten once, and you stayed in the room together, the room of which you were a leader, could you perhaps place it in time, the month or the portion of month when this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was -- that this happened during the middle part of our stay in the camp. I cannot say exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That means the middle, around the middle -- mid-point in your stay at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that you were in Keraterm about two months and five days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixty-seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I see, 67 days. So the mid-point would be early July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a few days up or down the calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, during your examination in chief, you said that when you arrived at Keraterm, you found five or six men from Kozarac who had been detained and that there were 10 to 12 guards at Keraterm. Can you tell me how this guard duties worked in those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that anybody really knew how this worked. They were coming and going. Most of them were reserve policemen. I only recognised the policeman Kosta among them. Then some left; others came. I have no idea what was going on. But there were always some people there; that's about what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Regarding the persons who you saw there, and one person that you knew, were all these reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I didn't know many of these people who I saw there. Later on, I saw Kajin and then things changed a little bit. Kajin had his unit and I think that the unit was brought there to provide security. This is what people were saying. And this came out of conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Regarding this period, were incidents frequent during the period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in those days, except the things that -- Zigic had this special treatment group or a group for special treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The way you gave evidence here yesterday and today, some guards left, some guards arrived. I take that to mean that it was fairly loose in terms of the shifts and all that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those early, first days, nobody -- nobody really bothered us or there weren't any major incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: During the period when you saw these guards, before the three shifts were established, and you also mentioned this group for special treatment.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Given your overall experience, including your national service and whatever you know from your civilian life about the military and police organisation, can -- could you say that there was order and discipline in those days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no discipline. Well, I don't know. I don't know about this group for special treatment, and I don't know about this military discipline. Perhaps there was no need for anything like that. We talked, we had contacts, except when there was beating, then there was no talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is what I'm driving at. You were referring to some people as shift commanders and let's say just plain guards. Could you make a comparison between them and the hierarchy and organisation in a professional police force or military force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you could not make such a comparison. That was not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me whether you knew or had met Tomo Prodan who was in security of Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew Tomo, and he was there at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know what his role in the camp was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was some kind of a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mean shift commander of some kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember anyone who was on guard duty on his shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a person called Krelac. He was not from Prijedor. He had a long cable, I think an electric cable, pretty thick. He beat people with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your assessment, if you can help me by trying to remember approximately when the three shifts were introduced, that is the 12-hour shifts that switched off, as you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may have been 20 days into my stay from what I can remember but I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In these -- during these 20 days, can we say that Tomo Prodan was in this position of a shift commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please tell me whether you know whether you saw, heard that some higher-ups came to the Keraterm, that is, hierarchically above Kole, Sikirica, Fustar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zivko, who was a retired policeman, I think he was superior to them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Zivko Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know him but I heard about him from others who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about it? What do you mean by saying that he was superior to all of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I cannot, but he came dressed in a suit, with an overcoat on his arm, in a Mercedes car like a boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did he come frequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not frequently. And again, let me say, I never saw him once. I only heard about him having come.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that from the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that Zivko Knezevic ever reviewed the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that in this first period before the third shift was formed, Tomo Prodan was also present at the camp as one of the commanders. What I would like to know is whether you know that towards the end of June something happened with the shift in a sense that somebody Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. left that so-called duty, that somebody took it over.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how correct this was, but I know that at one point, Tomo was no longer around, and there were three shifts. Kole became one of these shifts, and Kajin and Fustar were already shift commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you now please tell me -- I will read something to you. Can you -- and if you can tell me whether this is correct that you testified about your detention in the Keraterm camp and that you've given the following statement so far. This is from the statement you gave on 23 August to the Tribunal investigators. This was the 23 August 2000. Witness statement, you say, "This statement is for the previous statement made by me enlisted below." And then listed as one statement and then in brackets an ERN number is given, 00262312-00262313 dated 8 November 1993 made to the Bosnian authorities. "I read this statement on 23 August 2000. This statement is accurate." Then listed as number two, statement dated 6 November 1994. Again, in brackets, I am going to skip the ERN numbers, made to the Bosnian authorities. "I read this statement on 23 August 2000. This statement is accurate except for page 2, paragraph 6, line 10 where the word broken and it should read built." Listed under three, statement dated 19 January 1995 made to ICTY investigator Stephen Upton, "This statement is accurate except it says page 6, paragraph 2, line 2, this should read Kole beat a Serb who had beaten prisoners." That is --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who attempted to beat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And number 4, "In addition to these statements, I recall being spoken to on 9 June 1999 by Hans Oelvebro. I had notes made by him read back to me and I found these notes to be accurate." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this statement of the 23rd of August 2000 to the OTP investigators, did you confirm that they were your statements, you read them and signed them and are they all accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But if you read them and put your signature underneath?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this, I should like to ask you the following: Yesterday, during your direct examination, when the Prosecutor asked you, you answered the beating of Drago Tokmadzic, Ismet Kljajic, Esad Islamovic, Edin Islamovic and a Serb called Jovo happened during Kajin's shift. Could you tell me how is it that it was during Kajin's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Banovic, because he was on his shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you mean it is because there was a guard, Banovic, and that is how you identified the shift as Kajin's?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and Keli too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I see. It was through Banovic and Keli that you decided that it was that shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And since you mention Banovic and you did so yesterday, you said that there were -- that he observed no shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That he used to come by day or by night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whenever he needed something on his private business, whatever, he just came.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But would you then allow that it was possible that it wasn't Kajin's shift when that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was many years ago. All I can say is that Keli did not -- at least I don't think he came during other shifts, but it is quite possible that that had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you also answered questions asked by the Prosecution and said that the guard Keli on Kajin's shift beat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what do you know that it was Kajin's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it was Kajin's shift precisely because, after that, it came to a stop. That is, it happened on a number of occasions, whenever Kajin arrived in the camp, incidents would stop, and that's how I know that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You mean that somebody had reported that Kajin was on his way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was night-time because it happened at night-time, and the car -- the headlights as they entered towards Keraterm, you can see them as arriving from Cirkin Polje and they already know who that is and everything stops. That is, those things stopped at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what month was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the latter half of my stay in the camp. It was the latter half of my stay there. It could have been a month and a half since my arrival there, thereabouts, perhaps a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, during the examination in chief, the Prosecutor asked you some questions and you answered that on Kajin's shift, that brothers Banovic, Keli and Kajin's brother were all part of the Kajin shift, and that Fustar's shift included Baltic, Kondic and Cigo. Is that correct? We didn't hear an answer. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the statement you gave to the Bosnian authorities on the 6th of November, 1994, number 2, 6 November, 1994 and you said that you read it and signed it, thus confirming its authenticity, its accuracy, and you say there on the first page: "There were three guard shifts in the camp. The leader of one of these shifts was Damir Dosen called Kajin." Then you list: "The shift also included his brother, Drazen or Drasko, his elder brother, Bosko Baltic called Cvrco from Urije Prijedor, young, has a big hooked knife, he used to work for Bosna Montaza in Prijedor. Brothers Banovic, Nenad and Predrag." And then you go on to explain, "Predrag Banovic called Cupo."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't quite sure about their names at that time. I wasn't sure about that, but I couldn't have stated it as it is written because I do know Bosko Baltic rather better than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me just finish. In that same statement, you said that Fustar's shift included Zoran Cica and Cigo. And now in relation to what you told us previously, according to this, since on page 4 of this statement you mention Fustar's shift, Kondic, Baltic, Cigo and others. Now, when we juxtapose it to your previous-- to what you affirm previously in the same statement, Kondic and Baltic were members of Kajin's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there must have been a confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no, it is not correct. Baltic was not on Kajin's shift. He was a member of Fustar's shift; I'm quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also said that Kondic was on Fustar's shift. In this statement here you put him in Kajin's shift. That is, in the statement that you gave to the Bosnian authorities in 1994.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's a mistake. It was a mix-up or perhaps I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you told us that you had read this statement and signed it as accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was read out to me and perhaps I wasn't listening all that carefully, or perhaps I didn't hear well, but that is -- there are already some corrections. Some descriptions are not correct. So there could have been also a mistake which occurred in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But this statement was given to Bosnian authorities. There is no translation. So it was in your mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, right, well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So may we then suggest that -- at least say that these two statements are different, that they are contradictory, and yet nevertheless both of them say that they are accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you have made your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Likewise, in your statement to the Bosnian authorities on 6 of November, 1994, same number as before, on the first page you list the guards on Kajin's shift, which I read out to you a moment ago, and I see here that guard nicknamed Keli is not mentioned here. Then in the next passage in the same statement, you mention Keli. I shall read it out to you to see how -- "I was mostly beaten by Keli, fair-haired, tall, about 180, about 26 or 27, has patch with the Serb trhee-colour on his shoulder, and he also had a bandana with the -- those three colours." If we agree that, as against the previously listed guards, you described Keli in greatest detail, and yet you do not put him on Kajin's shift, how is it that you forgot to list him as a guard on Kajin's shift on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a formal statement. I never prepared myself to give any statement. I didn't prepare now. And I'm saying only that I know and I was responsible. Perhaps at that time he simply skipped my mind or perhaps he as an individual didn't skip my mind but I couldn't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you nevertheless identify him in the sentence before you describe Keli, "I was mostly beaten by Keli," or, "I was worst beaten by Keli," so he should stick in your memory, shouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember his name and then it just came back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I need to ask you this because I have just told you, you also confirmed that this statement was -- had been read out to you, that you had signed it and that it was accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is gospel truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: For the first time in your statement to the investigators of the OTP, or more accurately the first statement was given in 1994, the investigators' notes, 1999, and this is the statement of the 23rd of August, 2000, so it is -- this is the first time, in the year 2000, in eight years after Keraterm, you mentioned for the first time that there was a guard called Keli in Kajin's shift. Can you explain how is it that you never mentioned him before? And is it correct to say that you are not really sure which Keli [as interpreted] he was on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Keli worked in Kajin's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then how do you explain that after 8 years, you put Keli on Kajin's shift for the first time notwithstanding a number of statements that you had made. And you told us that you had read each one of those statements before, and signed them, confirming their accuracy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to explain it really. Well, let's see. I first said that I just couldn't really remember him, and you have him in this earlier statement so you see it is noted down. You just read it out a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But can you then explain it to me how is it that eight years later you suddenly remembered him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, the Chamber will deal with alleged contradictions and inconsistencies. Once you put what you consider to be a contradiction or inconsistency to the witness and he gives his explanation, there is really no need for you to take it further. It is then for the Chamber to assess the explanation that has been given. I mean that is the classical rule of a judicial body. You identify the inconsistency, the witness gives his explanation, then it is for us to assess the explanation and to say whether we accept it as true or not. There is no need to drag the matter on ad infinitum. Now let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Likewise, during the examination-in-chief yesterday, you said that during your stay in Keraterm, you had been beaten twice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also, on the same occasion yesterday, said that the first time you had been beaten by a military policeman, and my question is: Could you be more specific in terms of time, when did it happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it happened after only a few days between the two events.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. My question is when did this first military policeman beat you? You told us you had been beaten twice. The first time it had been a military policeman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know. This time -- we didn't really think much about time so 10 days, give or take 10 days, I mean. I really don't know. I can't be very precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. But can you be -- can you give us approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was in mid-July, thereabouts, give or take a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when Keli beat you, which was the second beating, according to you, how long did it happen after the first beating, after the first beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several days. Well, it could have been five days later, thereabouts. I'm not really sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, I should like to go back to the -- to what you said yesterday about that military policeman who had beaten you. You said that he was a tall man of strong build, from Sarajevo, that is Sarajevo Novo, municipality of Centar, that his father's name was Ilija. You also saw his identity card because he had shown you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You also testified that it happened during Fustar's shift; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is accurate too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then you also said that on various occasions, Fustar told this policeman not to beat you on the head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And did this policeman obey?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not really. He hit me on the head and by my head and wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please, I know these are not happy memories for you, but could you be more precise and tell us where did he strike you? For how long? How many times in front of Fustar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it went on for about 15 or 20 minutes, but it wasn't nonstop beating. He would put his demands to me and then beat me again. And so it -- he hit me around area and on the shoulders as he stood in front of me. He would just wave his baton and hit me wherever it hit me, and that was the police baton that he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But could you roughly tell us how many times that he hit you on the head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the head, well, 7 or 8 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I should now like to put it to you that in your statement to the OTP investigators, that you said that you had been beaten twice. However, here, in this statement, in this statement, you indicated that you were beaten -- that the first time you were, "... beaten by a policeman from Prijedor, and I don't know his name. And the second time, I was beaten by a man called Keli." Now, isn't it true these two statements are at discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I've never said that. I'm sure of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Then how do you explain that? And you say that you never said anything like that when you also claim that the statement was read out to you or that you had read it and signed it as accurate, as we have already noted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know if you are aware that these interviews take a long time. They last very long, and one gets tired. And at long last when the statement is read out to him, you don't hear half of it. But I agree that it should -- that everything should be as it should be. And I always stated that he was from Sarajevo, that he was a big man. He showed me his ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it right that in comparison with your first statement, with your yesterday's testimony, in your first statement to investigators, you did not mention that Keli was on Kajin's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've settled that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've been through this, you know, about which shift Keli was on. We really have heard a great deal of evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, just a moment. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us more specifically something about the time when, according to you, Jovo, the Serb that you mentioned, was beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really say with any accuracy. I could not do that. Perhaps other people know the exact dates and all that, but I, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you give us an approximation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean it happened. It happened in July, sometime mid-July towards the middle of July, well, possibly, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement to the Bosnian authorities in 1994, you state that, "He was beaten by brothers Banovic, Nenad and Predrag, by Kondic, Cica, and Baltic." And in the investigator's notes of the 9th of June 1999, you say, "Cupo Banovic, Keli and Goran Lajic beat a Serb called Jovo." And you also said that you, in particular, recognised Lajic's voice. And after that -- so these are two. And then yesterday, in the courtroom, you indicated only Banovics and Goran Lajic as the individuals who did that beating.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do not know why I really have to be so precise about every name, and whether I can remember all the names. I suppose it is not possible to remember all the names, but I'm quite sure that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree that all these statements are different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there are some slight discrepancies, but they come down to the same, and what I said is gospel truth. It was Banovic who used a baseball bat to beat him, and so many bones were broken. Everybody knows that. Well, it doesn't really matter who was on whose shift, they were moving around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I wasn't speaking about shifts. I simply said that in various periods of time, you identify different people. On three different occasions you gave different names of people who had done this. Would you agree that these three statements are different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statements are not different. I do not agree with that. There are some slight differences.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in view of the time, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much longer do you have, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I suppose up to half an hour, up to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Hopefully you will be able to, perhaps, conclude it in a little shorter time. We'll take the break now and resume at 11.30. Witness B, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody including the members of the Prosecution team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I appreciate your suggestion and I will cut short my remaining questioning. It will last less than half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Witness B, when I asked you about your first beating by the policeman from Sarajevo and you described how this happened, you said that he received blows in -- to your body and you received seven or eight hits on your head with a police baton?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the Bosnian authorities of 6 November, 1994, this is what you stated: You describe how the military policeman from Sarajevo arrived, you give the same information, "and ask me to find him two extremists. Because I did not point at anyone, he beat me by hitting me about 50 times with his baton over the head." Is it correct that there are discrepancies between the two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are discrepancies. This second one is more accurate. I don't know how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But you said that this was an accurate statement and you signed it as such; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me ask further, concerning the taking out and beating of a man whom you described as an ethnic Serb called Jovo, whom you did not know, and my question to you is as follows. In the statement of 6 November, 1994, given to the Bosnian authorities, you stated very precisely this: "Sometime around 25 June" -- sorry. "In Keraterm camp, Jovo Radocaj was killed. He was an ethnic Serb from Laskarci. He was married to a Croat woman, a man who voted for a sovereign and independent Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Do you agree with me that this is what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is what I was told, that this was so. It is true that I did not know him, but I stated what I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me now point to you the first interview you gave to the Tribunal investigators, the OTP investigators, of 19 January, 1995. That means about two months after you'd given the first statement. And this is what you say: "That same night, a man was brought to the camp, who was also killed. This was an ethnic Serb called Jovo, whose last name I do not know. He was married to a Muslim woman and lived near Hambarine. At the elections before the war, Jovo did not vote SDS but rather gave his vote to the SDA, and this is why he was killed." Do you agree with me that this statement differs from the statement, the previous statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, what is stated there is different from the statement that I gave to the Bosnian authorities, but the Bosnian authorities knew from other statements that this was so and this is what they wrote down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, though, that you signed both these statements and stated that you had read these statements and that you had signed them as your own?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My next question to you, and I'll take you back to the event of the 24, 25th of July, and the shooting that occurred. Could you approximately put the time frame to that, those shootings? From what time to what time did these shootings last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was very late. There were three intervals. It ended maybe two hours later in time, maybe two, two and a half hours, maybe even three hours, these three intervals. I don't know. To us it seemed so long. To us it seemed like 100 years, not two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you say that it -- that the shooting stopped before the dawn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, before the dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And you're certain about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, the morning after the shooting and after the massacre in Room 3, when men came out of the rooms to collect the bodies, can you tell me whether there was any shooting at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was no shooting. No, there was no shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So did you hear any shooting at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, perhaps somebody did shoot, but I did not register it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That morning you came out of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the door of the room when Kajin came and opened it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this in front of the door outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our door was a little bit set in. There was like a little entry way, hallway, and then -- about a metre long, and then the door was at that depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you just one additional question. In your statements you described in detail Zoran Zigic, and you said that among other things, you knew that before the war, he had killed a man in Prijedor and that also he had killed a woman. Do you know who this woman was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That happened during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know that was Kajin's cousin, his uncle's daughter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness B. Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it may assist the court with respect to the previous statements that this witness has provided to either the Tribunal or to the Bosnian authorities, we have copies of those statements available, if those would be of assistance to the Tribunal in assessing the alleged inconsistencies that my learned colleague has just pointed out to the court. If those would be of assistance, we are happy to provide those and ask that they be marked as exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we think that would be helpful, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have copies for all the parties. It has been previously disclosed to the Defence. We do have copies here, including a complete set for the Bench. We would ask, however, that they be under seal for the simple reason that there is information contained in the statements that would tend to identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They will be under seal. Mr. Vucicevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. With your permission, if I may stay here because I spread my notes and statements here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And also with your permission, if I may conduct the examination both at times in B/C/S and at times in English, and you will note at the times why those switches might be preferred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness B, good morning. Yesterday, you identified Dragan Kolundzija, Kole, and you said that you had known him for a number of years. Do you know that he played on a team, soccer team from Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And you said that you, too, were a sportsman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did you play for a team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I played for the team from Puharska.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any matches between the local teams between Puharska and Cirkin Polje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and there were also friendlies.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the team from Cirkin Polje did not have their own field, their own stadium, but rather played their matches in Puharska and used as their home field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they used as their home field.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that Kole was not the best player on his team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps Petrovic was. He also played for us for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree with me that Kole was the captain of his team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure myself who was the captain at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a Muslim, whose last name was Sulejmanovic, [redacted], played on Kole's team against your team and other teams in the territory of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sulejmanovic, I'm not sure that I can remember that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was a Muslim that was on Kole's team at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So you say there was such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If he was from Puharska, and was not on the Puharska team, does that mean that his qualities as a player were below the level of your team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that wouldn't mean that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Is it possible, and, in fact, probable that Kole, as the captain of his team, helped a Muslim to play on his team?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: My questions -- this line of questioning is through the assistance of Kole. He asked me to ask you these things.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: My friend, Rodic, reminded you of the statement you gave on 19 January 1995 to the investigators of this Tribunal, and the investigator was Mr. Stephen Upton. The last page, you said this, I quote: [In English], "Kole worked for a few days after the shooting but lost his job because he beat," and first you said "guard", but later on you corrected it in your August statement of 2000, so correction stands, "... but he lost his job because he beat a Serb who was trying to beat a prisoner." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so far as I know this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you see that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know at what time, approximately, what month, what week this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened after the incident, after the massacre, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about this incident, and from whom did you hear it, and when did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it in -- during those days and I was told that a Serb had tried to come in and beat Muslims, and Kole did not allow him and then finally hit him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How did he hit him? Did he kick him? Did he punch him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did he resist? Did he hit back at Kole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I only know that Kole did it. This is what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, in the same statement which I gave to Mr. Upton in 1995, you said as follows, [In English] "When Kole was in charge, he would let the families give food to the prisoners but he was the only one that allowed that to happen." Yesterday you also testified that it also happened on Kajin's shift. Yesterday you also testified that after some time, after a short period of time in the beginning, there were blankets that were allowed. There were blankets that were allowed to be brought in to the prisoners by their families. Did you make all of these statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember today that Kole's shift was one, among others, that were allowing blankets to be brought in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kole's shift when -- once it was established, we already had blankets. But new inmates were coming in and Kole did allow for them to also be provided with blankets. After the interrogation was finished on the upper floor, he allowed phone calls to be made so that we would be brought -- we could have food brought to us. And in this way, the word spread around about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now that you mentioned Kole's goodwill and his willingness to enable you to make phone calls, in one of the statements given to the OTP you said that after the massacre Kole allowed you to call home, to you, personally; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: On that day when you were allowed it, all the families in town, naturally, were worried about what was going on with their own. Did he allow this to you or to others?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He gave permission to me and to a young man called Pearson, this is what we called him. I called home and I said that everything was all right. I want to thank him for this. He also gave permission to some other people, people whom he knew well and with whom he was on good terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: There is a small detail which is that after this incident, Kole did not come to the shift for several days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Kole, after that, was no longer the shift commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean since you gave evidence that on the morning of the 25th the door did not open until late in the morning, does that mean that Kole had already left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you recall now when did you make a phone call to your own to tell them about where you were? Was it on the first day or after several days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on the first day. After several days. The first day we didn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could it have been on the second day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Second or third.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Fourth even?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fourth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But you are sure that Kole -- it was on Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was Kole himself who let me go and do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that in these -- in such circumstances, sometimes it was very difficult to perceive or memorise when something -- remember when something happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may seem that it was right after something happened, but it could have been several days later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement given to the Ministry of the Interior, the MUP, here it says that it was taken in Travnik in November, 1994. However, in one of the statements which you signed, in August, 2000, it says it was 1993. Can you tell us when it was? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, 1992, that was when you gave your first statement? When was it? Because here it says it was given in 1994. In the other one it says it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: August, 1993, would -- could not be possible. Believe me, I'm not sure when I gave it, but in 1993, that is entirely possible. It is possible that it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion you said, among other things, as follows, describing a scene that was going -- that took place on the afternoon of the 24th of July. It's the last paragraph. I will read it out to you. However, I have the English version. [In English] For the benefit of the easier presentation to the court, I would read in English. "The reserve policeman from Prijedor, Grujic, also known as Grujo, walked behind him holding an automatic rifle. On my way back from the kitchen, carrying bread, I saw camp inmates standing in three circles with 10 to 12 people each on the meadow in front of the hall." [Interpretation] I would like to point out to you, to draw your attention to the word you used in this statement, which is "kitchen." Can you describe to -- for the Trial Chamber where this room was, and when you went to fetch bread, was that the regular time of when you were receiving food or was it something out of the ordinary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: This kitchen, we did not use the kitchen, even though that was the entrance to the kitchen. That was the door to Room number 2 before the toilet. Under the staircase we had a table and this is where we prepared lunch. This lunch was not served at the same time but it was rather dependent on when it would be delivered, and so then we would go about distributing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: However, on that occasion, this was a year or 18 months later, after the -- after the fact, your recollection of it was fresher than now, or maybe not. Was this during the regular lunch-hour or did you go to get this bread a little bit later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was quite a bit later. I think that this would be past the regular dinner time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Would you have been able to go after a regular meal was served, go there and see if there was any additional food or did you need special permission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day we were not given regular lunch but we saw that there were some preparations, and Fustar's shift was before that, and during their shift we were kept under lock. Then this man Jakupovic and I went and we brought this bread in a plastic container, and distributed among men in Room number 4 where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Would you describe for the Trial Chamber the size of that container, basket? How big was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well it was plastic, it was this size, about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So let's say 50, 60 centimetres in length?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say 80 centimetres in length, and the breadth would be 40 to 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And how deep?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thirty or something.
