utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Was this sliced bread, cut bread, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was sliced.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So that was bread which had been brought that day but you, in that room, had not received any?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bread was delivered every day. We would slice it there. There were always two female cooks and we assisted them in slicing this bread so that it would be done as soon as possible. On that day they did the slicing themselves and waited for the lunch to be distributed. It was never distributed that day. I don't know what happened to the other rooms but we only got the bread, and somebody said, "Go get the bread, they will give us bread." And we did, even though it was a bit dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to offend you in any way but there were some other soldiers on the perimeter. You said that that was -- this was happening during the worst shift. If you recall, did you go on your own initiative or did you ask for permission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not need to ask for permission. The shift had changed over, so this was Kole's shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So it was Kole's shift already?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the shift had taken place. Kole's shift was on duty. Grujo was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But there were two Grujo's.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a tiny Grujo in blue police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But this Grujo could also be sometimes in another shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't think so. He was there from the beginning in the camp, and he initially was in another shift before the three shifts were organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just -- a moment ago we established with regard to time perception, it is very difficult to say something positive after all that time. Yesterday you said that those men were beaten during Fustar's shift. Let me finish. Then you said today, while I examined you, that the door was locked at times during Fustar's shift. Do you remember now, that afternoon, was your door closed during Fustar's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it wasn't locked. We did not come out, but they always made us go in just when it occurs to them, just get in, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted]. The doors were never locked in daytime. And I already said that beating began during Fustar's shift and it was cut short and there were some new blokes. I'd never seen them before. A number of them wore red berets and I didn't really -- I wasn't really allowed to look at them. I simply passed by them very quickly going to fetch bread and I never had cause to look at them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: However, in all your statements so far - and there were five of them - and during your testimony yesterday, you invariably said that no beatings occurred during Kole's shifts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And that then includes the 24th? There was no beating that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Kole's lads did not beat anyone but those others beat those men. Now, how was it, why, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You, in your statement given in August -- and I shall read it out to you -- I shall read out to you what you said and I shall read it out to you in Bosnian. This is it,"I know that Kole's shift was on duty in the night when prisoners in front of Room 3 were massacred. Earlier that evening I had gone out to get bread, and it was then that I talked to Kole. It was a conversation about general matters. We realised that something was afoot at the entrance. There were soldiers; they were not just ordinary guards. It was evident that something was in the offing. I asked Kole to lock us up in our room." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that, and that is how it was. We were locked up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And whenever he came to take over the shift, Kole would, that is what you told us, unlock and locked the door again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: The door was locked at 9.00. It wasn't always Kole himself who did it. It did not really matter. The doors were locked and the keys taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: However, and this is also with a view to identifying the periods of time when one could see something, perceive something. This is a very important detail, don't you think so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be. It should be, yes. It ought to be very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: However, on the 8th of November, 1993 as you told us yourself, and how -- although it says 1994 here, and these -- this statement was given to an authorised official attached to the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina whose name was Zijad Ibric. And you signed that statement, you read it. This is an important detail. You never mentioned it in a single word, never. Then you gave a statement on the 5th of November 1994 and, again, a statement given to Mr. Ibric with much more specifics. You even mention a policeman from Sarajevo who showed you his ID card, and yet you do not say anything about the so-called preparations. Then you also made a statement on the 19th of January 1995 to Mr. Stephen Upton, an investigator in the OTP here. And again, you say nothing about that detail. Not a word. Then you gave a statement on the 6th of September 1999 to Mr. Hans Oelvebro in the presence of Mr. Kapila Waidyaratne, one of the Prosecutors. And here you immediately start off with the gunfire opened of Room 3, time and the rest, you do not mention any soldiers or any preparations. And earlier you said that your brother, your elder brother; what is the difference, a year or two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little less than two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You said that he was with you all the time throughout, that is, you were arrested together, and you were released together. And I guess being brothers you also had adjacent pallets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have any pallets at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But you did have some blankets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and styrofoam.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And as your brother, he is a man of great integrity, isn't he? And if he remembers something, he will say so, won't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will wrap it up, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the report of the 15th of August 2000, made by your brother to the Prosecutor, this is what he says, [In English] I apologise, but I do have an English version here. "I didn't see any of the preparations made prior to the massacre of the men in Room 3." [Interpretation] Now, if you saw something going on, wouldn't you have said so to your brother, if nobody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he had not seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: That was all I wanted to ask you. Could it be that the bench with machine-guns that you mentioned yesterday, but never before that, that it was the next day that you saw them rather than that evening? Could it have been that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they were there that evening too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The Prosecution has no further questions. I would just like to ask for clarification from the registry with respect to the exhibit number for the witness statements that were tendered a few moments ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does the registrar have the numbers? Yes, please give them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The numbers will be -- the witness statements of the date 23 August 2000 will be Exhibit 6. The witness statement of the 9th of June 1999 will be Exhibit 7. The witness statement given on the 19th of January 1995 will be Exhibit 8. The witness statement given on the -- that's stated in the statement the 5th of November 1994 will be numbered Exhibit 9. The witness statement given on the 8th of November 1994 will be Exhibit 10. This is number 02/273. The last one will be also dated the 8th of November, 1994, number 02/272. This will be Exhibit 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness B, that concludes your evidence. You are released except for this, the statement that was handed to you and on which you will provide some information. Mr. Mundis, would you provide the witness with the statement? I think it's Exhibit 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- so he can make the notifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And just for clarification, once he has returned that document to me, then he is free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My learned friend and I have discussed the list together. I have two slight amendments to make to the requirement that I was going to ask the witness to do. Can my learned friend and I either speak outside or I can cross across the Court, if it's not discourteous to you, and just inform him what the requirement is. Would that be acceptable to Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, please take the statement over to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the matter that Mr. Greaves and I discussed, that's what you want me to give him at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And he can go outside and mark it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I approach my client for a second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly, the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I call the next witness, Your Honour, I have a brief application to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness did not seek -- we have not sought any protective measures for this witness so far. I wish to make an oral application now for facial distortion and that a pseudonym be granted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And the grounds?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has family who reside in the Prijedor area. In particular, he has an elderly father and a brother. He visits his elderly father quite often and, Your Honour, he has concerns for his father and his brother, and also his own safety should his identity be revealed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would be the happiest man today if I could join my learned friends in their "no objection", but this application would be -- really wouldn't make any sense whatsoever because it is being placed at this time. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise for interrupting, but it may be appropriate that we move into closed session if we are going to deal with what I anticipate my friend is about to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let us move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps a time will come when these changes can be done electronically. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness, could you have a look, please, as this piece of paper that I'm about to show you? You can see on that piece of paper your name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And do you also see your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness, I want you to understand that in these proceedings you're going to be referred to as Witness C. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I tender that document. Your Honour it will be Exhibit 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, can I take you back, please, to the early months of 1992. At that time did you reside with your brother in a town called Puharska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, except that is a section of the town of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Without mentioning the name of your brother, did you live in the same house as he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And did you have another brother who lived in Puharska in a separate dwelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And is the town of Puharska in the opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. It is part of the Prijedor town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: At that time, that is, in 1992, what was the population of Muslim persons who resided in that town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: In Puharska, the Muslim population was about 10.000. And for the town of Prijedor in whole, it was about 50.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Are you, yourself, a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can I take you back, then, to those early months in 1992. What was happening to the Muslim persons in the area of Puharska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: On 30th of April, the Prijedor SDS, that night they took over the power, in front of the municipal building Serbian flags were hoisted. Checkpoints were established. They were set up on the approaches to the town. And propaganda, if I can call it that, started. That was broadcast on local media and local newspaper called Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was the nature of that propaganda?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: This propaganda was pointing out that all the Muslims who did not want to put on uniforms, JNA uniforms, could not go to work anymore. They were being fired from their jobs. Their healthcare benefits, their social benefits were taken away from them. Their presence in workplaces was no longer desirable, and it was during that time that we started being fired from our jobs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Without telling us what position you occupied, were you working at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And were you able to attend work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No. As part of all this, Muslims were limited in where and how they could move because we ran a risk of being checked at these checkpoints, mistreated, harassed, and so on. And I want to underscore this, we were forbidden to go to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, you've mentioned checkpoints. Whereabouts were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They were set up on the -- on the perimeter of town, on the approaches to the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, were those checkpoints manned and, if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They were manned by JNA soldiers. In fact, these were the Prijedor citizens of Serb ethnic background who were wearing JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, what would happen to persons of Muslim ethnicity when they encountered a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: We had to identify ourselves, so to speak. In other words, we had to hand them identity cards so that they could see who we were. Then they would ask us, well, why we were going to town, what was the reason for it. And in April they would let us through and we could move about with these controls.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You mentioned not being able to attend your place of employment. What was the consequence, insofar as medical care was concerned, of not being able to attend work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: By the very fact that we did not go to work, we received no salaries which also mean that we did not have the benefits that come with that, pension, healthcare and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, can I take you now to the 30th of May in 1992, that is, after the attack on Prijedor. Did something happen in the area of Prijedor on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: From my house I heard from the direction of the Prijedor old town great noise and something like shattering. And when we climbed upstairs, we saw that that part of the old town was on fire. It was in flames.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you refer to "that part of the old town", what town are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Prijedor. That part of town we called "old town".

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: On that day did something happen to the Muslim and Croatian people residing in the town and, if so, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I later learned that Muslims from that part of town were evacuated, and I had an aunt who lived there. Muslims from that part of town and from a part of town around new hotel, they were all evacuated. They were placed in buses and taken to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, what was Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Trnopolje was a camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would ask that the Court move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, I want to take you now to the 31st of May, 1992. Did something happen to one of your brothers - and please don't mention his name - on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. My brother was taken away, alongside the other citizens of Puharska and they were taken to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was that the brother with whom you lived or was it the brother who lived in a separate house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, the one who lived in a separate house.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you see him being taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. From my house, from the window, I saw him being taken away, and how they took his car from the garage.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Who took him away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you've learned that he was subsequently taken to the Keraterm camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I take you now to the 12th of June, 1992. Were you at your home with your other brother on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And did something happen to you and your other brother on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Sometime around 3.00, we had lunch, and I went to my part of the house. About 15 minutes later I heard banging on the door, and this older brother called me, yelled at me to open it up. I opened the door, and I saw about 10, 12 soldiers with their rifles trained at me. I was confused. I only recognised a neighbour of mine, who was a reserve policeman. He pointed a rifle at me, and I said, "What is this? What is this all about?" I can't mention the name of this neighbour. I was confused as to what was the reason for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What ethnicity was this neighbour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think he was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And were there any other persons with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. There were about 12 soldiers with him. They told me to come out. Some soldiers went in to search the house, and the others were surrounding the house, and when the two of us came out, the whole group of 12 soldiers gathered together. One went to search the house and -- one part went, and the other part, among whom was my neighbour, ordered us to board a van.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: From which army were those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They were wearing JNA camouflage uniforms, but there were some in police uniforms, because my neighbour was a retired policeman, so he went back on duty. He had a blue camouflage uniform. And perhaps a couple of other of -- other soldiers had them too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You've referred to a van. Can you describe that van, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: It was a van that had a driver and a passenger next to him. It was -- that had only passenger seat next to it. It was sort of like a freight van. This neighbour came in -- they told us to get in, and we stepped in and we had to sit down on the floor because there were no seats. I believe that the van was yellow.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were there any other persons in the van when you entered it? [redacted]. When we boarded the van, a kombi -- the van went further into Puharska and collected another man, I think that his name was Mesic and he was an agronomist. I think he was beaten. My brother and I were not beaten. This Mesic was beaten very severely. They beat him up badly and they threw him in the van.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Of what ethnicity was this person you've referred to as Mesic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Mesic, he was a Muslim. All four of us who were in the van were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: We were taken to the MUP building, to the Prijedor municipality MUP building. That's where they took us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: We were ordered to get out and to kneel down on the pavement, to lean against a wall of the building, with three fingers spread out, and to continue to kneel until we were told otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: For how long did you kneel in that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour or an hour. And meanwhile, this neighbour and my brother were taken away, allegedly to be questioned. When my brother came back they said that they were also beaten and abused.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you yourself questioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No, I was not. I think a man came by who I think knew me and he asked me whether this was me. I said yes, and then he said, "Stand up. You don't need to kneel down." And I wasn't taken in for questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, you indicated you were required to kneel while resting your body weight upon three fingers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you place any significance to that particular procedure, that is the three-fingered --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. That was a special salute that Serbs used. The soldiers used it. That is how they saluted each other.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, what happened after you left the MUP building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: We were placed in a police van, blue van, and I sincerely thought that we were being taken back home. We could not see where we were heading, but I sort of knew the direction that we were going because of my familiarity with the town. When we arrived at the cross -- at the intersection of the Banja Luka road, I realised that we were not being taken back home, that we were being taken somewhere in the direction of Banja Luka, and it was then that they took us to Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if that would be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it would be. We will take the adjournment now, resume at 2.30. Witness C, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. Mr. Ryneveld, perhaps when we return, before we begin the evidence, you could provide that information which I requested, or are you not yet in a position to?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I will certainly be able to do that when we resume at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 24 25

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honours, whilst we're waiting for the witness to return to Court, can I deal with the list that we asked to be marked by the previous witness, Witness B?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Witness B has now carried out that exercise, I think, in company with Mr. Mundis. There are three pages which we seek to have exhibited to the evidence of that witness. He marked on one page only, one name, and inscribed the bottom of the page in his own language. I've given a copy of that document to one of the interpreters who I think can translate what is written at the bottom of the form for us, and it can then be read into the transcript if Your Honours are agreeable to that procedure. Perhaps my learned friend could confirm what I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Again, just to clarify and make sure that the record is clear, you will recall before the witness withdrew that Mr. Greaves approached the Prosecution table with a slight revision in his request, and that revision was that the witness only be shown three pages of what was previously marked as Exhibit 6. And so rather than the witness being shown the entire logs that he maintained, he was shown three pages and on those three pages he did, in fact, mark one name which he then inscribed a note at the bottom of the page in his language indicating that that individual from his room had been killed during the time that he was in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Is that what you want to be translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No. There is -- three lines in the witness' own language were inscribed at the bottom of one of the pages. One of the interpreters has a copy of that document and perhaps he could just read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could those three lines be read by one of the counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Witness C, in his testimony so far, has used the word "neighbour" about three times identifying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you just let us conclude this point, and then we'll come to the point which you are making. I think the interpreter was about to translate something, and then we'll come back to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In fact what the interpreter has done has asked one of the Serbian speaking counsel to read the phrase, and perhaps my friend, Mr. Londrovic, would be so kind as to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LONDROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Witness B saw the document which was shown to him in the presence of my learned friend, Mr. Mundis. And he wrote in his own hand the following text: "The person whose name I circled was killed in Keraterm while I was there (he died in the room 7 days after the beating)". And then there is the signature of Witness B and the full name of the person whose name he circled is Jasmin Ibrahimi. There are three pages, and the last three figures are 496, 497, and 498 are the numbers of the pages. The ordinal number of all the prisoners who were detained in Keraterm are from 1 to 138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you now wish to have those tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: My learned friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll make it 5A.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps we could mark the original which Mr. Mundis has in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Witness C in his testimony so far has mentioned several persons whom he had identified as "my neighbour." I would respectfully submit that in presenting the foundation for this witness' testimony, the Prosecutor introduce those names. It would be extremely helpful for us to prepare our cross-examination, number 1, and number 2, at a later stage, to perhaps seek the evidence -- information that could lead to evidence for the Defence case in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I don't think you can tell the Prosecutor how to do her work. When you come to cross-examine, then you can seek to get the name of the neighbour and we can then make a decision on that issue. So that's the way we'll deal with it. Mr. Ryneveld? Or Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was just inquiring -- prior to the break you had requested once again an answer to the "common-purpose" question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the Prosecutor's position that the common-purpose liability extends to all three of the accused with respect to conditions in the camp. Obviously, with respect to the genocide charges, only the accused Sikirica stands charged with those, but with respect to the conditions in the camp itself, the Prosecutor's position is that all three of the accused are liable under the common-purpose doctrine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, to the conditions, and of course to all the beatings and the murders and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and as Your Honour will recall, this matter was addressed in depth in pages 38 through 45 of the Prosecutor's Pre-Trial brief that was filed on 13 October, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, before the break, we had got to the stage in your evidence when you had -- when you arrived at Keraterm camp, having been arrested on the 12th of June, 1992. What time of the day did you arrive at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Sometime around 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And the van that you were in entered the camp and went toward one of the rooms in which you were subsequently detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The van entered the camp, stopped by the weigh hut. There they handed over some papers and then the van took us to Room 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Is it the case, Witness C, that there were four rooms at the camp in which detainees were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And were those rooms commonly referred to as Rooms 1, 2, 3, and 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Quite right, quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: For how long were you detained in total at Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Fifty-five days.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In which room were you first placed when you arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Room number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you subsequently move to another room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: For how long were you detained in Room 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: In Room 2, I was for about five or six days in that room, and then I realised that they were terribly beating and taking out prisoners from that room. And in Room 1 there were detainees who had been interrogated, and those from - I don't know how to put it - from the town itself, and they were, if I may put it that way, were treated slightly better.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: As a consequence of discovering that fact, did you move rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. I then moved to dormitory 1. I managed to find about ten centimetres of space on the pallet, and that is where I settled, together with my brother. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How was it that you were able to move rooms? Did you have to seek permission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, not really. I suppose they wouldn't have allowed me had I asked for that, but from time to time, depending on the shift, one could move around, that is go from one dormitory to another. It wasn't much of a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: In August of last year, that's in August of the year 2000, did you make a statement to investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor for the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. During the taking of the statement did you draw a sketch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to draw a rough picture, drawing upon my memory of what did that camp look like.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I'm just about to show you a two-page document. And I have, Your Honours, copies for Your Honours as well as my learned friends. With the assistance of the usher, might the witness be shown this two-page document?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, does that appear to be a copy of the sketch that you drew? That is the first page that you're shown, and on the second page you'll see a notation in which your name is redacted. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the original of that sketch is available in court if Your Honours wish to peruse it or indeed my learned colleagues wish to. Might the first page of the sketch be placed upon the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, can you look, please, at the document on the ELMO? And you'll see there that you have marked a building as a reception. You used the word "reception." Can you see that building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: This here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was that room used for during your time at Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That room was mostly used by the camp commander, Sikirica, Mr. Sikirica, and shift leaders, that is Kole, Kajin, and Fustar. They were there mostly, or when they needed to talk to guards, that is where that took place, while I have to mention that whenever detainees arrived, they had to go across this weigh bridge to get here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, you've also marked on that sketch two things you've called "machine-gun emplacements." Do you see those two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I do, yes, yes. Here in front of Rooms 3, 4, and the other one in front of Rooms 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you arrived at Keraterm camp on June the 12th, were those machine-guns in place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You'll also see on the sketch two things that you have marked "search lights."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. They were not there when I arrived. Those search lights were installed later on. I cannot remember when exactly, but it could have been some 20 days after my arrival or so, but be that as it may, they were put there at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, you've given some evidence that you were first detained in Room 2. Can you focus now, please, on Room 2 and describe that room to the Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Room 2 was larger than dormitory 1 or, rather, it was the largest of all the dormitories and it was roughly, I've indicated here, about 20 or 25 by 20 metres. In the beginning it had a tin-plate door so that in the evening, if you closed the door, you couldn't see anything outside. When I arrived there, it wasn't filled to capacity. Perhaps it was less than half full. There were pallets inside and that is where we slept, on those pallets.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Given a measurement as to the width of that room being 20 metres, and I think you said it was also 20 metres deep; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, thereabouts, 20, 25. Perhaps it wasn't square. Perhaps it was longer than it was -- perhaps its length was bigger than its width.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, how did that room compare to this room, that is, to this courtroom in terms of its size?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, I'd say that it was of roughly the same length, but it was likely wider. From glass panel -- from glass panel to glass panel, that was the -- its length, perhaps slightly longer, but it was wider.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How much wider?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, say about 5, maybe as much as 8 metres. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you turn your attention, please, to Room 1. You've said that you were detained in that room and you, on your sketch, have marked that it was 8 metres wide and some 20 metres deep; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I should say so. I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How did that room, in terms of its size, compare to this room, that is this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, say, it was not as long. Say from the beginning of this desk to the glass panels, more or less. And it was much narrower. From this partition behind me to the Judges' bench, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And were you referring to the table in which the Prosecution lawyers are standing -- are seated when you referred to the first bench?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No, no, no. I meant that table over there and roughly to those window panels. Perhaps a little less. No, say from the beginning or -- the beginning or the end of this table to the glass panels. It was shorter, anyway, by about a couple of metres than the Room 2, and it was much narrower than Room 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And the table to which you referred is the table upon which the court reporters are sitting, the people typing at the back of the room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, say behind there, behind their desk. Roughly from the beginning of that table to the end of that table.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly, it occurs to us that at some stage we'll have to have some information on the measurement of this room.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I imagine you have that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, can you describe, apart from the size of that room, can you describe Room 1, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, again, in the beginning it also had a metal door so when you shut it, you couldn't see anything outside. But later on they put another door with metal bars so that we could look through and we had more air. It was easier to breathe in there. Inside there were pallets lined up on the left, and one on the right, and in the middle two lines, two rows of pallets the whole length of the dormitory, and that is where the detainees slept.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did the detainees have any bed clothing apart from those pallets upon which to sleep or upon which to cover themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, we didn't. Those who were lucky found pieces of cardboard to put on those pallets. And the -- those who were lucky ones to find something like that to make those pallets slightly softer. And we had nothing to cover with unless some of us had brought something along from home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is a pallet? What is it composed of?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you understand the question? What exactly is a pallet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I'm about to. Since Keraterm was a tile factory before the war and also refractory tiles were made there, the pallet it was more or less 120 by 100. It was at about this height, and a forklift would enter to put these tiles and then take them around various areas or plants in the Keraterm factory. On the top it had boards some 10 centimetres broad which were also separated by some 10 centimetres and simply lined there. So that is where we could lie down. As a matter of fact, when there were enough of them, those who were lucky enough to find those pallets to lie on them. In the beginning there was nothing, and at that time we had to lie on the concrete floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What were those pallets made of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Wooden boards.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, can you focus again, please, on the sketch on the ELMO. And you will see, Witness C, to the left of Room 1 you've drawn and arrow and what appear to be stairs. Can you see that? To where did those stairs lead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. These stairs led to the offices which were on the upper floor, and that is where the interrogators who questioned us were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, you've also drawn on your sketch some WC notations which I take it they refer to the toilets; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How many toilets were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, I think there were four, three or maybe four. I'm not sure. But that I can -- I think that was their number, three or four, and then were the squatting ones, three or four.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did the detainees have free access to those toilets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No. Well, it depended on the shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What did the detainees use to relieve themselves when they didn't have access to the toilets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Room 2 had a barrel in a corner, and the inmates relieved themselves in it when the shift leaders -- or rather the guards locked the door at twilight. And dormitory 1 did not even have that, so we had to relieve ourselves in bags. And then we discarded those bags next to a door to try to prevent the smell from pervading the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I tender that sketch, which, if it's admitted, will become, I think, Exhibit 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, I want to take you back now to your arrival at the camp. Before you were detained in Room 2, were you searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived - and I think it was Kole's shift - Kole searched us. Later on I was told that we were lucky because usually the majority of inmates was beaten during that search. We raised our hands. Whatever we had in our pockets we placed next to us on the ground. He searched us, and I was given my identity card back. And then we went to Room 2. He told us to go to that dormitory number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was the person you've described as Kole, Dragan Kolundzija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I recognise him. I just recognised him now. In fact, I recognise them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Well, just -- can you just listen to the questions that I ask you and don't do anything that you're not asked to do, all right? Did you know Kole prior to your detention in Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How often did you see this person Kole in the camp while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I would mostly see him when he was on duty, which means fairly frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you describe him to the court, please, as he was in 1992 when you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I'll try. For instance, he was probably a little taller than I was, well-built. He was good-looking. He kept his hair short, brown, maybe a bit darker. He was wearing the so-called SMB colour uniform. And gentle features, I'd say. That's about -- a good-looking face. I don't know how else to put it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How tall are you, Witness C?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: 185, 185 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Are you able to say how old he was at that time? Just estimate.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I don't know how -- what his age would have been, but I think that he was younger than I was, maybe about 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You've referred to him as being a shift leader. I'm going to ask you some questions about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: -- the personnel in the camp who were guarding you. Firstly, were you able to observe any particular pattern or organisation in so far as those guards were concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. There was a camp commander, Dusko Sikirica, that is. Before him, there was -- Sikirica came later, maybe 15 days into the existence of camp. And before him there was a retired policeman; I think his name was Zivko Knezevic. Short, stocky, I remember him well. And then later on Sikirica came. And there were three shifts. Shift leaders were Fustar, Kole, and Kajin. And then after that there was another one, Tomo. I don't know whether he came later on or what. So there were three shifts, three shift leaders, who had somewhere between 10 and 12, depending, guards, soldiers, who were subordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, what observations did you make that drew you to conclude that the -- those shift leaders were the superiors of those guards who you say were subordinated to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That was very simple. The keys to these dormitories were with the shift leaders, and they would lock and unlock them. And they were the ones who ordered the other guards what each one of them was to do. In other words, they were giving them assignments.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you say they were giving them assignments, or as you said, orders, what exactly -- what kinds of orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I don't -- I couldn't tell exactly what types of orders exactly, but the changes of shift were taking place in this area which I call the reception area, this hut. And then when there were some tasks to be carried out, for instance, when somebody was to be taken out, then they would issue them orders, and anyone could conclude that on the basis of their mutual relationship. For instance, when the food arrived and the inmates would be lined up, or when there was any other activity in the camp, these three men would issue orders and they would issue them to the guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And did the guards appear to obey these orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you see it working the other way as well; that is, did you see any of the guards reporting to the shift leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. That was a relationship of a subordinate and a superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, so far you have described Kole to the court. What I'd like you to do now is to look around this court and see whether you recognise Kole. Do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think that he is on the far right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When you say "the far right," what I'd like you to do is to identify him in terms of the seat in which he is seated, counting from left to right. What seat is he in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Seat number 5 at the far right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And is that in the far row?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You've said there were three shifts. Did those shifts correspond to any particular hours during the day and/or night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. I think that at first I was a bit unclear about these shifts. I thought that they would be leaving at 6:00, but in fact they would leave at 3.00. However, later on, this functioned better. I think that they had longer shifts. I think that there were three, 12-hour shifts. I think that that is how they worked, and this is how they rotated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You've referred to Kole as being the leader of one of the shifts. Who were the leaders of the other shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: After Kole's shift, I think it was Kajin's shift, and after Kajin's shift, Fustar's shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Is the person Kajin also known to you as Damir Dosen? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. His nickname was Kajin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you know that person before you were detained at Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Very slightly. I may have seen him in town, but just in passing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you describe him to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think that Kajin was a little bit taller than Kole, more masculine features, perhaps more pronounced, and tall and slender, of athletic build, brown hair.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Looking around the courtroom today, are you able to see that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Again, in terms of the seat and the row he's in, can you identify, counting the seats from left to right, can you identify what seat he's in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Far row, seat number three.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I would ask, Your Honours, that the record reflect that the witness has identified the accused Dragan Kolundzija and the accused Damir Dosen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, you also, in your evidence earlier, referred to a person you called Sikirica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you know that person prior to your detention at Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was that person's position within the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: He was camp commander, that is, he was the number-one person in the camp, and shift leaders showed him respect and treated him as a camp commander. And guards had a little -- showed a little bit of awe towards him. So they really had a lot of respect for him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What observations did you make that led you to conclude that the guards had a lot of respect or awe for him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: On one occasion when I received some food, and I had gone over to the gate as I indicated, and when the guards saw that camp commander was arriving in the car, he said, "Get lost. Get lost. The commander is coming in the car. We can't have you being seen here."

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You said that you didn't know that person prior to your detention in Keraterm camp. While you were in the camp, how often did you see this person Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I once saw him at the entrance when I stayed there at the gate, and he arrived. And after that I only saw him in passing, not very frequently, when he was on his way to that office where the interrogations were taking place. I don't think that he ever came close to where these dormitories were, didn't approach that area very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, ever have any face-to-face contact with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No, no. Except at the entrance gate when this Kum of mine came and brought me some food when the guards told me to get away.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I'll turn to that in a moment. But for the moment, can you describe this person you say Sikirica as he was in 1992? The way you saw him in the camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Sikirica was shorter than either of the two of them, that is Kole and Kajin, and he was shorter than I am. So he was let's say about 175 centimetres tall. He was well-built, more muscular, and he was also darker brown hair. The face was a little bit rougher. I think I mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What clothing did he wear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: He was wearing military uniform, a so-called SMB, dressed as a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did he ever wear any headdress or anything on his head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: A hat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What kind of a hat was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think it was a military-style beret or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What colour was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: So far as I can recall -- in fact, I don't know. Maybe the same SMB colour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you ever see him without that cap on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I think he also walked about without it. I may have seen him without it on several occasions too.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What colour hair did he have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Let's say it was brown, perhaps a little bit lighter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You've said that in terms of his face, his skin was a little bit rough. Did you notice anything -- any other distinguishing features in relation to his face?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think he had a moustache at that time, so far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Do you feel, Witness C, that you would be able to recognise that person again were you to see him today? You have to answer orally.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you look around the courtroom, please, and see whether you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, seat number two. That is where he is seated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And, again, is that in the back row?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, in the back row in the second seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I would ask that the record reflect that the witness has identified the accused Sikirica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, Witness C, I'm going to turn now to the conditions in the camp and to the activities that would take place during the day and the night. Firstly, what would happen in the morning, say at around 9.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Let's say at that time, for the most part, we were allowed to go in groups of 10 to file out to the toilet. And this depended on the shift, actually, not in every shift. And also it depended on what had happened the day before.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Firstly, in relation to the shifts, are you saying that one or other shift was better than another in terms of being able to use the toilets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Which shift was the better shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: For instance, Kole's shift was the best. It was better than the others.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And can you explain what you meant by "depending on what happened the day before"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: For instance, there were times when the Serb troops were going to the front line or coming back from the front line. Then they would be shooting from the road, the main highway, which I indicated. And we were not allowed to go out in order to prevent some incidents from happening, and depending on which shift was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did anything else take place during the morning hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The shifts were changing around 6.00, and then the interrogators would come sometime between 8.30 and 9.00. And then at 9.00, interrogations would start, that is, a soldier would come with a piece of paper and names would be called out, and then the inmates would be questioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Were you yourself ever questioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Where did this questioning take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: This took place in the offices located above Room 1, approximately there, on the top floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And who did the questioning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: These were -- are you interested in the names?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: If you know them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Just pause there. Were these questioners guards at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Who are you referring to? No. These were interrogators, those who were questioning us. They were, I don't know how to call them, inspectors or investigators.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: So far as the guards at the camp are concerned, did they play any role during this interrogation process?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think they did not, except for the one with the piece of paper who would come, call out our names, and then escorted us up to be questioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did either Kole, Kajin, or Sikirica ever do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think they did not, or perhaps infrequently. It was mostly this one soldier who would bring this paper, while the investigators worked upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You said that you yourself were interrogated. On how many occasions were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I was interrogated once in Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That was approximately perhaps 15 or 20 days after my arrival at the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What questions were you asked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No, that is -- that was silly. Where I was, what I did, whether I was a member of the party, whether I was politically active, things like that, absurd questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: During that process, were you mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I was not. My brother was, but I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you some questions about the camp conditions. Firstly, the food. Did you receive food while you were in the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: We received some kind of water, sometimes there was some potato or beans or some kind of noodles in it. It was some kind of a broth. We received it only once a day. And with that, there would be a single slice of bread, provided you were not the last one. Because even that food was not sufficient for all the inmates to be fed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Of what quality was that food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Oh, poor, poor, of course it was poor. It was hot water, hot soup.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you've indicated that there was insufficient of that food for the -- for all of the detainees. What happened to the detainees who -- when the food ran out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, they had to go when the food ran out, and they had to go back to their dormitories.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Whilst you were in Keraterm camp, did you -- what happened to your body weight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, I lost about 15, 20 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You said you were fed once a day. Can you describe the feeding process, just briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, they -- it was per dormitories, 1, 2, 3, 4. Then 1, 2, 3, 4. Then 4, 3, 2, 1. And that is how we alternated. And the caldron was as I showed on the sketch. It was next to this wall, to the WC, in front of dormitory 2. And what would you get? You'd get a bowl or something. You have to eat it very fast -- well, depending on the shift. But by and large, you had to eat it very fast and then wash it, return it, and depending on -- sometimes you couldn't wash it and then give the bowl to the next inmate, and that's how it went on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: During that procedure, did you ever see a person by the name of Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. That was a bloodthirsty one, and he was often in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Who was Zoran Zigic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I knew him before the war. He used to drive a taxi. I mean, I knew him by chance. He was a taxi driver. He was very short-tempered even before the war. And I know that he was brought to justice for a murder before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You said it was very bloodthirsty when he was in the camp. Can you describe what happened when he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, say, for instance, if we are having lunch, if he and Duca turn up, that was a sign for us to disappear, to vanish from that place, to get back into our dormitories as fast as we can. If we don't manage to do that, then they select 10 or 15 inmates and start to beat them, to mistreat them, kill them, and the rest. At any rate, we were terribly afraid of him because we knew that chaos would start the moment he turned up.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How often did you see him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Very often, very often. In the beginning perhaps more often, and then towards the end of the camp less so. Only from time to time, because I think -- at least that was the story that went around, that he had also -- that he was also detained behind the dormitories because he had committed some offence or other, and he was also serving a term. But be that as it may, in the early days of my detention, he was there very often. He did as he pleased. He really could do as he pleased. And whoever he wanted to take out on, he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did he appear in the camp on all of the shifts or only on some of the shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, let's say he turned up during all the shifts, but perhaps he couldn't really terrorise on all the shifts. Sometimes more, sometimes less.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was there any particular shift on which he could terrorise less?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, I think that, for instance, during Kole's or, say, Kajin's shifts, he really couldn't do that or at least while there was still some daylight.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Who was the leader of the night shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the rotation of the shifts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: By that do you mean that shift leaders would alternate between the hours they worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, yes, as the shifts changed so they would leave. 12.00 the next shift arrives and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You referred to a person by the name of Duca or Duca, who was that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I did not know him personally before the war, but I heard that he was a butcher by profession. I know he was short, very stalwart and like Ziga or usually with Ziga. They'd come together and he also terrorised the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was his full name Dusan Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Dusan Knezevic, I think so, yes. Dusan, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You've spoken about the food. What about water, drinking water? Did you receive adequate drinking water whilst in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Not in the early days, and we mostly had to use the water that was there for industrial use. There was a manhole in front of the third room or near the WC, I think, and there was the hose, the hose used to wash the WCs when they were washed. Then we'd pour that water into bottles, or whatever we had, and later on, towards the closure of the camp, water systems arrived with drinking water.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you describe, please, the conditions that prevailed insofar as personal hygiene, that is, washing bodies and clothes is concerned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, I'll use my example. After 32 days I managed to get a bath. I had a sweatsuit on me, and in time it got so dirty and torn that I simply had to cut off its legs and turn it into shorts. I mean it was horrible. After about 20 days of my detention in the camp, I think lice infested us. We were all infested with lice, all over our bodies and hair. And then it depended on the mood of the shift leaders that we could have a bath or not. As I told you, I had this bath after some 32 days. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There were no showers -- well, towards the closure of the camp, yes, it became slightly easier so that we could shave or something. No, the hygienic conditions were nil. It begged a description. Simply how one could keep people under such conditions and how they survived under them, it's still beyond me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, insofar as the health of the inmates was concerned, was there any consequence of drinking that industrial water that you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, we often contracted dysentery from that industrial water. That was really horrible because in Room 1 there wasn't even that barrel, and the inmates had to relieve themselves in bags which we then left at the entrance so as to be able to breathe at all. And it just -- depending on whether an inmate had been beaten or not. If he had been beaten, he'd just relieve where he was. So the stench, I mean that place reeked of stench, and it really is indescribable. I don't know how people could live there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: This question, technically, is incorrect and it calls for expert opinion and not a speculation from the witness. Where we went with this answer, the answer was not responsive, and I ask it to be stricken or another question to follow to fit the answer. Because dysentery is not, and could not be a result from the industrial water, and we don't have evidence -- we don't have a foundation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I think it's within the witness' competence to provide the answer to the extent that he can. If you wish, you can cross-examine on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, you've given some evidence about what took place during the day at the camp. What took place at night-time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: All this wouldn't have been so difficult had it not been for the nights, and had it not been for the call-outs. On those occasions, and I repeat once again, depending on the shift. But then guards would come and beat with -- beat against those bars in the door of the dormitory and call out some of the inmates, and then they would take them over here to where dormitory 4 is near this garbage dump and that is where they beat them, battered them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How often would that kind of thing take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, on the average, every two or three nights, they would call out between 5 and 10 inmates, that order of things.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What happened to those inmates who'd been beaten after they'd been beaten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: It depended on one's physical health and when his turn came to be beaten. Those who were physically weaker and those who were the first in line, they would stay there. And some of the inmates, probably those who were fifth or sixth in line when those had already got tired, then they did have a chance of being -- of getting back to the dormitories and we'd give them water, try to wash them a little, to help them come to. Some of them died. Some of them survived.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did any of them ever receive medical attention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I saw, I think, two or three times, I'm not sure, perhaps even on more occasions, that some of the inmates who had been injured were taken away, I guess to the hospital, somewhere to get some medical aid. But I say that, I think, only on two or three occasions. By and large, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, I'm now going to turn to some specific incidents that took place in the camp, and the first incident that I'd like to ask you about is an incident when your best man, or the man who had been the best man at your wedding, visited you in the camp. Do you recall that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Do I?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When was that, in terms of your stay at Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, it was about, I don't know, perhaps about a month after I arrived in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: One of the inmates called me and said, "Somebody is looking for you at the entrance. Go quickly." So when I reached the entrance, I saw my best man, my kum. He had come with his wife and his two children, to visit me. And he was the one who had asked me to come to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what happened when you came -- when you arrived at the entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: And when I reached the entrance, well, we stood there for about five or six minutes. And then I saw his -- that his wife had brought a bag with her, a bag full of food. And of course I was looking at that bag. I wanted to get at that food. And of course we chatted there. Meanwhile, however, a car appeared, and the guards cried out, "Get lost, the camp commander is arriving -- is coming." And there I found myself in a very awkward situation. I could not leave and leave the bag behind. And so as he was drawing near, I just stayed there. And he went through the entrance and went to this reception office, and then turned back. He turned back -- now, I don't know. He said, "What's it? What's new?" or something, he enquired of those guards around there, and looked at me thinking, well, this is my best man, he's a Serb, he works in the paper packaging factory. That is, I said all that. Simply all I had in mind was to get my hands on that bag with food. And that is why I was there. And Mr. Sikirica allowed me to stay there. I suppose -- I don't know if he recognised my best man or whatever it was, but he let me just stay there. And he then went back and I stayed behind for another 15 minutes with that best man of mine, and it was then -- and I took the bag. It was then that I got hold of that bag.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: After you'd got hold of the bag, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: And then I took this asphalt path on the -- on the left. I started for dormitory number 1. And from the reception office this path is slightly higher, and as I looked right, I saw Sikirica, and as I was moving, as I was descending, I could see, looking sideways, that there was an inmate in front of him. I believe that he was kneeling. And I was moving towards the dormitory 1, and when I had fetched up there or just passed by, I heard a shot. And of course, I was panic-stricken. I thought, "Oh, my God, they have killed me." But then when I passed by, I just turned to the right to see what had happened. And I -- then I heard -- very well, do you want me to go on or --

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Just pause for a moment there, Witness C. What time of the day or night was it when this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think it was around roughly, in the afternoon, between 2.00 and 3.00, 2.00 and 4.00, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was it in the daylight hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
