utterances.text: What did you see when you turned around after you'd heard the shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Then Mr. Sikirica was saying -- I think he uttered an obscenity, and then he said, "This is how every inmate who tries to escape will fare. I shall personally settle the score with him." And I think the movements he was making looked like -- looked as if he was putting back his pistol where -- I'm not really sure because when I heard that shot, I turned mechanically and that is what I heard, quite well, and I think he was putting back the pistol in the holster behind his belt or something.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you see the inmate to whom you've referred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: As I was passing by, before that I saw him on his knees in front of him. I did not know that man. I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: At the time after you'd heard the shot and when you turned around and you saw what you thought was Sikirica returning his weapon to his holster, did you see the inmate at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Where was the inmate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, at that time he wasn't there -- I mean, he had already fallen down on the ground -- to the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Could you see what had happened to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I think he was shot dead. I mean, that was clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How far away were you from Mr. Sikirica at the time when you saw this incident, that is saw him returning his gun to his holster and the inmate fall to the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, say, there was this path between us. It could have been some eight or ten metres on the right-hand side from where I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And how far was this inmate who had fallen to the ground from Mr. Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: He was right next to him, next to his feet.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I'd like you to look at a series of photographs, and these are photocopies of Exhibit 2. If you would just firstly look through those photographs and see whether you can identify a photograph that shows the area in which you saw this incident take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, for instance, this photograph perhaps, maybe, and maybe this one, but this is from very, very far.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you choose the best one, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Perhaps this one? Just a moment, please. Well, no. I think this one would be the best, slightly clearer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Just pause there for a moment. I'm going to give you a pen. What I'd like you to do -- what I'd like you to do on that photograph is mark with an X please where you were when you saw this incident take place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No, I can't do it on this photograph, this one. I walked like this and I was here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Just pause there, please. I just want you to put an X where you were when you saw Mr. Sikirica returning his gun to his holster and the inmate fallen to the ground. Have you done that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you place a Y, please, on that photograph where Mr. Sikirica was at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, here, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And can you place a Z, please, where the inmate was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not seeing them, Ms. Baly, the Y and the Z.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Can you attempt to make the -- them a little bit clearer, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is my X, this is my Y, and this is Z here. On the grass he -- the two of them were on the grass, on the grass next to this road.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I tender that photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Exhibit 14, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, I'm going to move on now. Just -- those photographs might be returned. Witness C, do you know who that inmate was who was apparently shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I don't. However, from the -- from my later conversations with inmates, we learned that it was not one of those three inmates who had tried the escape. It was - that is what I learned later on, he was a pilot. He really was a pilot who had lost his mind and simply wandered around the camp. He had no self-control, and I suppose that the guards must have planted him as the man who had attempted escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Was there a time, Witness C, when a group of detainees from the Brdo region arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: It was much later, say late July. After the 20th, I should say, after the 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Where had those detainees come from, apart from Brdo? Which villages in particular?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. Those were Stredica [phoen], Biscani, Rizvanovici, Rakovcani, Hambarine, Zecovi.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And are they all villages in the Brdo region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How many detainees were there that arrived from -- who arrived from Brdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, those who managed it to Keraterm, they were -- and this is just a guess on my part, they were about 200, maybe 250 detainees, two or three buses, two buses, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What became of those detainees after they arrived at the Keraterm camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: When they arrived, those of us who were already senior inmates, we sort of already learned to guess what would happen to them. They would be in front of Room 3 during the day. They were there in the sun. A lot of them became dehydrated. They were not given water. And they kept them there. They would keep them there for four or five days. During the day they would lie in the grass in front of that dormitory, and then at night they would lock them up in the dormitory and they would not give them either food or water. They did not receive any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly, it would be very helpful if we could conclude the examination-in-chief today. I think, with the cooperation of the interpreters, perhaps another how many minutes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, well, we'll try. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C -- I'll try to move as swiftly as I can, Your Honour, through the next -- for the concluding part of the witness' evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, an event that has been referred to as the Room 3 massacre took place. I'd like you to focus upon that event. Where were you when that took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I was in dormitory 1 on the sixth or seventh pallet to the left inside the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did the event take place during the night-time hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Describe, if you will, to the Court what took place.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Sometime around midnight, approximately, we heard that something unusual was going on outside. There was some kind of an argument, a quarrel of some kind, and by the noises made, there was -- it was clear to us that a number, a substantial number of soldiers were entering the camp. We concluded it by the clacking of their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, were you able to see what was going on or were you relying upon what you could hear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I mostly relied on what I could hear, but occasionally I raised my head and I looked in that direction, because dormitory 1 overlooked directly the tarmac clear out to the entrance gate to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What could you see or what did you see when you looked out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The floodlights were turned towards dormitory 3. We were sort of in semi-dark so we were not blinded by the lights. So I could see the troops around the reception area. They were coming from the entrance gate and they were taking positions there. By the noises and by the sounds made by the weapons and by their movements, we could conclude that they were taking positions in front in the camp, in front of these dorms.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What led you to conclude that there was a quarrel taking place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: This was the time of Kole's shift. He approached our room and said something like, "There's about a hundred soldiers out there. Nobody get up. Nobody raise your head. Better kill him because they would kill him." And he said something to the effect that he could not control the situation, and then he walked away.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What took place after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: After that, perhaps about an hour after these noises and after these soldiers' voices, and in this interim period, we heard Kole and these soldiers who had entered the camp quarrelling, arguing. An hour after these soldiers had taken up their positions, we heard singing coming out of Room 3. The inmates in Room 3 were singing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What exactly did you hear in terms of the quarreling that you've Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. referred to said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, Kole argued with these people, with these soldiers. I don't know whether it had to do with these soldiers taking up positions when they were making this semicircle, but his voice was -- his voice was the dominant one. The argument went back and forth between him and these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was he saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: From what I could hear of those words that he said, he did take part in positioning of these soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, I want you to just listen carefully to the question. And the question was: What exactly did you hear Kole saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: For instance, approximately something like, "To the right. Not here. Over here. Don't do it without my order." Something to that effect. This -- there were different things said from the start to the end, from when the shooting started to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What was said when the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: When this terrible shooting started, it lasted for about 10 to 15 minutes, and then it stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Then, we could hear single shots, and then we could hear something of what these soldiers were saying, "Watch the one to the right. Shoot to the left. He is running to the toilet." And this is when you could hear these individual shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: What did you hear Kole say, if anything, at that stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: At that moment, I remember well when Kole said to the inmates in number three, "Break the windows. To break the door." Because apparently they were left without air in there. And what he was saying, and this dialogue with the soldiers, for instance, at one point they told him, "What are you meddling in? Let us kill them all. What are you meddling in?"

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did he respond to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I don't know now. I cannot say exactly what he responded. But for the most part, it was this argument. This was the -- that is how it went.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: When was it that you heard him say, "Don't shoot without my order," or words to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Between these intervals of shooting, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Doing the best that you can, Witness C, can you recall anything else, specifically, that was said by Kole during that incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: For instance -- well, in fact this is more or less it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, did you see the bodies of the persons who had been shot after they'd been shot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Where did you see those bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The next day, Kajin's shift took over, and they designated one inmate from each of the rooms to go to number 3 to pull out the bodies of those killed. A friend of mine from my room volunteered, and he went there. I could see that from the front of the room, I saw a truck parked in front of Room 3. They were bringing out the bodies on the grassy area in front, and then they loaded them up on to the truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And did the truck leave the camp with the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, it did. When they loaded up the bodies, they ordered the wounded ones to climb on top of the bodies. There were about 50 of them. They lowered the canvas on the canopy and the trucks drove away someplace.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The following day, did you see more bodies in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: The next day, during the night shift, there was again shooting in Room 3, and later on, from the inmates' conversations, I learned that those wounded inmates who declined to go -- leave, were then finished off, 15 or -- between 15 and 20 of them were then killed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did you see what happened to those bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: They were also loaded up on a smaller truck, another -- a military truck with a canopy also, and then it also drove away in some unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Now, Witness C, during the period after the massacre, did you have occasion to see a military truck enter the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes, very frequently, towards the end of the camp, before it was dissolved, military canopied trucks were coming to the camp, and they were asking for volunteers to go and round up livestock, also to gather -- to pick vegetables or fruit, and they were asking for volunteers, and people were also called out. These men were then taken in unknown directions and we have not seen them since.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, were you yourself ever mistreated in any way, apart from the conditions that you endured, whilst you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Approximately a month after my arrival at the camp, I relaxed a little bit, and what I mean by that is that I would venture out a little bit more often. And one night, around midnight, my brother and I were called out. We were in Room 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And what happened to you after you'd been called out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I responded. In fact, the basic thing was for someone to say that you weren't there, but anyway, I responded and I said that my brother was not there and that he was at Omarska. Then the man who called me out said, "All right. You come over here." I managed to put on -- and again, the important thing was to put on as many layers in order to sort of absorb the blows. So I put on some clothing and took my identity card with me. Then they said, "Go towards Room number 4, in fact towards the garbage dump." They were all masked. I could only see their eyes. And one of them said, "So you have a knife," which was nonsense. So I was walking towards Room number 3, and this is where I stopped -- no, Room number 4, in the direction near the garbage heap. And I talked to them constantly, and they were -- they were talking about my being [redacted], and I was saying, "No, no, no, that's wrong, I am -- I do the body work -- I have a body shop, I mean a -- I have a car business." And I said, "Look," and I said, "Listen, my best man was" such and such a man, and I would mention some Serb names that -- and I kept telling them how they were mistaken. All the time I kept saying how this was mistaken, and that I was telling them different things. And then one of them said, "Stop. Stop talking now. If you go on talking, I'll kill you now." So they took away my identity card at that time, and they started -- they huddled together, and one of them said, "Go back now." I ran back to Room number 1, and that is how it ended on that night.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Five, five or six of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Did they beat you in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Well, yes, they did. I did not feel the pain at that time. I just kept talking. I just kept saying, "No, no, no, I'm not that person." Only two or three days later, when I took my clothes off, my brother screamed and said, "What you have on your back?" And they were like these blue marks on my back from where I received blows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did they beat you with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I was lucky. They only beat me with a police baton. And they kicked me a little bit with their military boots.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, were you released from the Keraterm camp on either the 3rd or the 4th day of August in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: My apologies, can I just make a comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is it in relation to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: After that night, I was called out one more time, because they determined, I suppose, that I was indeed the person that they were looking for. [redacted] [redacted]. The rest were either killed or were transferred to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And did anything happen when you were called out that one more time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: I was lucky that time. I responded, and I said -- I said, "He is in number 4." So they went over to number 4, so they would -- went to look for me there. Then they would go to the reception, to see where I was. And these ten minutes, which is what it took, saved me because the chief of that shift, Tomo, came in a truck, and he was supposed to bring me with another soldier, and I was already reaching for the door handle and I thought it was all over. And at that point he had arrived, and he said, "What are you doing here? What is going on?" And they ran away. And this is what saved me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we are going to take the adjournment now until Monday morning. Witness C, you are reminded not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. Yes, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies for interrupting you. Witness C said that Tomo was the chief of shift, was in the van with Witness A.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C
utterances.text: No, no, I never said that, I'm sorry. You had mentioned Witness A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, do not say anything. Let's hear what the counsel is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness C did mention Witness A's -- Witness A's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ah.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Describing this situation, he did mention Witness A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If that is so, we will have it checked and take the appropriate action, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So I repeat what I said, Witness C: During the adjournment, until Monday morning, 9.30, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 4.29 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday the 26th day of March, 2001, at 9.30 a.m.
